source_title: Clinical Impact of Semaglutide in Patients with Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction
research_question: Does oral semaglutide affect cardiac biomarkers and metabolic parameters in adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a retrospective single-center cohort of 27 patients with HFpEF and T2DM, three months of oral semaglutide was associated with a significant reduction in BNP levels compared with the pre-treatment period, along with improvements in glycemic control, weight, inflammation, and cardiac structural markers.
population: Adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and type 2 diabetes mellitus who initiated oral semaglutide at a single academic center (n=27).
intervention: Oral semaglutide, initiated for type 2 diabetes management.
comparator: Within-subject pre-treatment period (same patients, three months before initiation); single-arm design, no separate control group.
outcome: Change in log-transformed B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) from pre-treatment to on-treatment period; secondary: HbA1c, body weight, C-reactive protein, left atrial volume index, left ventricular mass index.
result_summary: Log BNP was stable during the pre-treatment period (p=0.34) but decreased significantly during the on-treatment period (p<0.001); reduction during on-treatment was significantly greater than during pre-treatment (mean difference -0.35, 95% CI -0.44 to -0.11, p<0.001). Concomitant reductions were observed in HbA1c, body weight, C-reactive protein, left atrial volume index, and left ventricular mass index; CRP change correlated with BNP change (r=0.46, p=0.015).
short_source_excerpt: Log BNP remained stable during the pre-treatment period ... but decreased significantly during the on-treatment period
limitations: Single-arm pre/post design; no separate control or placebo group.
Small sample size (n=27) from a single academic center.
Short follow-up (three months on-treatment).
Observational, not randomized -- cannot rule out regression to the mean or unmeasured confounding.
uncertainty_notes: This evidence bears on the research question via a small single-center pre/post cohort; it should be weighed alongside larger and/or randomized comparisons of GLP-1-class therapy in HFpEF before drawing a corpus-level conclusion.
confidence_note: High confidence that the extracted result and PICO fields are directly reflected in the paper's abstract; not a confidence score for the underlying study's methodological strength or a corpus-level conclusion.

source_title: Effects of Semaglutide on Cardiometabolic Risk in People with Obesity, With and Without Type 2 Diabetes: A Retrospective Observational Study
research_question: Does semaglutide improve body composition and cardiometabolic risk factors in adults with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a real-world retrospective cohort of 70 adults with obesity (with and without T2DM), semaglutide treatment was associated with significant reductions in body weight, waist circumference, HbA1c, blood pressure, and visceral fat, with more pronounced glycemic improvement among participants with T2DM.
population: 70 adults with obesity, 42 with type 2 diabetes and 28 without, treated with semaglutide per current clinical guidelines.
intervention: Semaglutide.
comparator: Within-subject pre-treatment baseline; single-arm observational design, no separate control group.
outcome: Body weight, waist circumference, fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c (primary); lipid profile, insulin resistance indices, inflammatory markers, hepatic parameters, body composition (secondary).
result_summary: Semaglutide was associated with reductions in body weight (-9 kg), waist circumference (-8 cm), HbA1c (-1.1%), systolic blood pressure (-7.5 mmHg), visceral fat area (-30.1 cm2), and insulin resistance markers. Glycemic improvements were more pronounced in participants with T2DM; skeletal muscle mass was relatively preserved.
short_source_excerpt: Semaglutide treatment was associated with significant reductions in body weight (-9 kg), waist circumference (-8 cm), HbA1c (-1.1%)
limitations: No control or comparator group; cannot isolate semaglutide's effect from other concurrent lifestyle changes.
Retrospective observational design.
Predictor-of-response findings (baseline HbA1c, visceral adiposity) are exploratory.
uncertainty_notes: Bears on the broader obesity/metabolic-syndrome question, but as a single uncontrolled real-world cohort it should be read alongside randomized trial evidence for semaglutide's weight and metabolic effects.

source_title: Weight-loss dynamics with tirzepatide versus semaglutide
research_question: How does weight-loss magnitude and adverse-event profile compare between tirzepatide and semaglutide in real-world use for obesity and type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a large propensity-matched real-world cohort, tirzepatide was associated with greater and faster weight loss than semaglutide, with lower prevalence of gastrointestinal and systemic adverse events, and demographic variation in treatment response for both drugs.
population: Adults treated with tirzepatide or semaglutide for obesity/type 2 diabetes; 10,339 tirzepatide-treated and 10,339 semaglutide-treated patients after 1:1 propensity matching on age, sex, T2D status, baseline BMI/weight, index year, and follow-up duration.
intervention: Tirzepatide.
comparator: Semaglutide.
outcome: Maximum weight loss over 2 years (categorized into five response groups), weight-loss velocity, adverse-event prevalence (AI-curated from clinical notes), pre-/post-treatment disease-prevalence changes.
result_summary: Tirzepatide-treated patients lost more weight than semaglutide-treated patients (mean reduction 14.7% vs 10.8%, p<0.001); high-response rate (>=15% weight loss in year 1) was nearly doubled with tirzepatide (42.6% vs 21.6%, p<0.001), with faster monthly weight-loss velocity (2.54% vs 2.18%). Tirzepatide was associated with lower prevalence of GI and systemic adverse events. Women and White patients were more represented among high responders for both drugs; Black and Hispanic patients were more represented among minimal-response patients.
short_source_excerpt: Patients treated with tirzepatide lost more weight than those treated with semaglutide (mean reduction, 14.7 vs. 10.8%; P < 0.001)
limitations: Retrospective EHR cohort, not randomized; comparative effectiveness, not a head-to-head trial.
Adverse events identified via AI-enabled curation of clinical notes -- the curation method's own accuracy is not independently validated in this record.
Demographic-subgroup response differences are exploratory and may reflect access/prescribing patterns rather than biological response differences.
uncertainty_notes: Directly relevant to the corpus's 'Dual incretin therapies such as tirzepatide' subtopic as a head-to-head comparator to GLP-1 monotherapy; should be read alongside randomized head-to-head trials where available.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Tirzepatide for Recurrent Weight Gain after Bariatric Procedures: Real-World Evidence of Efficacy and Safety
research_question: Is tirzepatide effective and safe for treating recurrent weight gain after bariatric surgery or endoscopic bariatric therapy?
claim_text: In an observational cohort of patients with recurrent weight gain after bariatric surgery or endoscopic bariatric therapy, 24 weeks of tirzepatide was associated with substantial total body weight loss and was generally well tolerated.
population: 34 patients (26 female, 8 male) with recurrent weight gain after bariatric surgery (n=32) or endoscopic bariatric therapy (n=2).
intervention: Once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide, dosing range 2.5-10 mg/week, for 24 weeks.
comparator: Within-subject baseline (pre-treatment); single-arm design, no separate control group.
outcome: Percentage total body weight loss (%TBWL), waist circumference, BMI category shift, adverse events, at 24 weeks.
result_summary: Mean %TBWL was 18.1 +/- 5.6% (p<0.0001), with significant waist circumference reduction (p<0.0001); most patients shifted to lower BMI categories, with the majority reaching overweight or normal weight status. Adverse events were exclusively gastrointestinal (constipation, diarrhea, nausea), generally mild, with no treatment discontinuations.
short_source_excerpt: the mean percentage total body weight loss (%TBWL) was 18.1 +/- 5.6% (p < 0.0001)
limitations: Small sample size (n=34).
Single-arm design, no comparator group.
Short follow-up (24 weeks).
Authors themselves describe the evidence as 'preliminary'.
uncertainty_notes: A narrow but clinically specific slice of tirzepatide evidence (post-bariatric weight regain) rather than general obesity treatment; should not be generalized to first-line obesity treatment without further evidence.

source_title: Shifts in waist-to-height ratio categories within tirzepatide groups: a post-hoc analysis of SURMOUNT-1
research_question: Does tirzepatide improve waist-to-height ratio category in adults with obesity or overweight, relative to placebo?
claim_text: In a post-hoc analysis of the SURMOUNT-1 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, tirzepatide was associated with sustained improvement in waist-to-height ratio category compared with placebo, in adults with obesity or overweight.
population: 2,538 SURMOUNT-1 participants with obesity or overweight (BMI >=30 or >=27 kg/m2 with at least one obesity-related complication, excluding diabetes), with or without prediabetes.
intervention: Once-weekly tirzepatide (5, 10, or 15 mg) plus reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
comparator: Placebo plus the same reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
outcome: Shift in waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) category (<=0.49, >0.49 to <=0.59, >0.59, per NICE framework) from baseline to week 72, and week 176 in the prediabetes subgroup.
result_summary: At baseline, 89.8% of participants had WHtR >0.59. After 72 weeks of tirzepatide (10/15 mg), 16.7% achieved WHtR <=0.49 and 54.7% improved their baseline category, versus 9.6% with placebo. At 176 weeks, among participants with prediabetes, 12.2% achieved WHtR <=0.49 and 46.4% improved category with tirzepatide versus 9.3% with placebo.
short_source_excerpt: After 72 weeks of tirzepatide (10/15 mg), 16.7% of participants achieved a WHtR <= 0.49, and 54.7% improved their baseline WHtR category compared to 9.6% with placebo
limitations: Post-hoc analysis, not a pre-specified primary endpoint of SURMOUNT-1.
WHtR is a surrogate anthropometric marker, not a direct clinical cardiometabolic outcome.
Excludes participants with diabetes at baseline.
uncertainty_notes: Randomized, placebo-controlled source trial gives this record stronger internal validity than the other tirzepatide records in this batch, but the WHtR endpoint itself is a post-hoc, surrogate measure.

source_title: Comparative effectiveness of tirzepatide and DPP-4 inhibitors in type 2 diabetes with heart failure
research_question: How does tirzepatide compare with DPP-4 inhibitors on mortality, hospitalization, and cardiovascular outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes and heart failure?
claim_text: In a propensity-matched real-world cohort of patients with type 2 diabetes and heart failure, tirzepatide was associated with markedly lower hazards of mortality, hospitalization, heart-failure exacerbation, and major adverse cardiovascular events than DPP-4 inhibitors.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes and heart failure treated between 2022 and 2025 (8,956 matched pairs after propensity-score matching); prespecified subgroups for HFrEF and HFnonrEF.
intervention: Tirzepatide (Cohort A).
comparator: DPP-4 inhibitors (Cohort B).
outcome: All-cause mortality, hospitalization, heart-failure exacerbation, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).
result_summary: Tirzepatide was associated with a lower hazard of all-cause mortality (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.25-0.42), hospitalizations (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.48-0.57), HF exacerbation (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.33-0.42), and MACE (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.73-0.84). Subgroup analyses for HFrEF and HFnonrEF showed similar trends.
short_source_excerpt: treatment with tirzepatide was associated with markedly lower hazards of mortality, hospitalization, HF exacerbation, and MACE compared to DPP-4 inhibitors
limitations: Retrospective, non-randomized comparative-effectiveness design; residual confounding by indication possible despite propensity matching.
Active comparator is DPP-4 inhibitors, not placebo.
uncertainty_notes: A large, comparative real-world signal for tirzepatide in a cardiac-comorbid T2DM population; the very large effect sizes (e.g. HR 0.32 for mortality) warrant caution and comparison against randomized evidence where available.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Comparing measured and reported change in gastrointestinal symptoms after initiation of metformin treatment: a questionnaire validation study
research_question: Do self-reported and directly measured changes in gastrointestinal symptoms agree after initiation of metformin treatment for type 2 diabetes in primary care?
claim_text: In a Swedish primary-care cohort initiating metformin for type 2 diabetes, a newly constructed gastrointestinal-symptom questionnaire showed moderate-to-good agreement between measured and self-reported symptom change for most of six assessed symptoms.
population: 54 participants with type 2 diabetes in Swedish primary care (the MEMO study -- Interaction Between Metformin and Microbiota), assessed at baseline and after 2 months of metformin treatment.
intervention: Metformin treatment, with GI-symptom assessment via questionnaire at baseline and 2 months.
comparator: Within-subject before/after comparison; this is a measurement-validation study, not a controlled treatment-effect study.
outcome: Agreement (Spearman's rho) between measured change (difference between two timepoint assessments) and directly reported/perceived change in six gastrointestinal symptoms.
result_summary: Spearman's rho exceeded 0.4 for 4 of 6 symptoms: poor appetite 0.60 (95% CI 0.39-0.75), loose stool/diarrhea 0.58 (95% CI 0.37-0.74), flatulence 0.45 (95% CI 0.21-0.64), abdominal pain 0.45 (95% CI 0.20-0.65). Agreement was lower for nausea and vomiting, though numerically above 75% agreement, likely due to few symptomatic participants overall.
short_source_excerpt: The agreement between reported and measured change of symptoms, measured as Spearman's rho, was above 0.4 for 4 out of 6 symptoms
limitations: This study validates a measurement questionnaire; it does not itself estimate metformin's GI-symptom incidence, severity, or causal effect.
Small sample (n=54), single-country primary-care setting.
No comparator arm without metformin -- cannot separate metformin-attributable symptom change from other causes.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contextualizes' rather than 'supports'/'contradicts' because this record is about the reliability of a measurement instrument for tracking metformin's known GI side-effect profile, not a direct claim about whether metformin causes or how often it causes GI symptoms. Useful context for interpreting other metformin-tolerability evidence in this corpus, including the imeglimin-replacement record in this same batch.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's methodological strength.

source_title: Imeglimin as a Replacement Therapy for Metformin in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Experiencing Metformin Intolerance: A Retrospective Observational Study
research_question: Is imeglimin an effective and tolerable alternative to metformin in adults with type 2 diabetes who have metformin intolerance?
claim_text: In a retrospective cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes and documented metformin intolerance, switching to imeglimin was associated with meaningful improvements in glycemic control and a favorable safety and tolerability profile over three months.
population: 100 adults with type 2 diabetes and documented metformin intolerance, initiated on imeglimin monotherapy or combination therapy for three months.
intervention: Imeglimin (monotherapy or combination therapy), replacing metformin.
comparator: Within-subject baseline (pre-switch) versus 3-month follow-up; no active metformin comparator arm, since the cohort is defined by metformin intolerance.
outcome: HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), postprandial plasma glucose (PPG) (primary); body weight, lipid profile, renal function, gastrointestinal side-effect rate (secondary).
result_summary: HbA1c decreased from 7.96 +/- 1.56% to 7.35 +/- 1.02% (mean change -0.62 +/- 1.05%, p<0.001, n=77); FPG decreased by 32.18 mg/dL and PPG by 44.63 mg/dL (both p<0.001). Body weight decreased modestly (-0.81 kg, p<0.001); LDL cholesterol and triglycerides decreased significantly; eGFR remained stable (p=0.135); GI side effects occurred in only 2% of patients.
short_source_excerpt: Imeglimin demonstrated meaningful improvements in glycemic control, with a favorable safety and tolerability profile in metformin-intolerant patients
limitations: Retrospective, single-arm design; by definition the cohort cannot include a concurrent metformin-tolerant comparator arm.
Short follow-up (3 months).
Single-country/setting; generalizability not established.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contextualizes' rather than 'supports'/'contradicts' because this record is not a direct claim about metformin's own effect -- it is evidence about managing metformin's well-known GI-intolerance limitation, directly relevant to the corpus's 'Metformin and type 2 diabetes treatment' subtopic as a limitations/alternatives data point.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors in elderly patients with type 2 diabetes
research_question: Are SGLT2 inhibitors associated with renal and cardiovascular benefit, and what safety trade-offs, in elderly adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a propensity-matched retrospective cohort of elderly adults with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with significant renoprotective effects, particularly among those with preserved baseline renal function, alongside an increased risk of genital infections.
population: Diabetic patients aged >=65 years who received antihyperglycemic therapy at a single Taiwan hospital, 2021-2023 (9,915 total; SGLT2i users n=3,345, non-users n=6,570; 1,529 matched pairs after 1:1 propensity-score matching).
intervention: SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.
comparator: Non-SGLT2-inhibitor antihyperglycemic therapy.
outcome: Renal function (30%/50% eGFR decline), coronary artery disease, ischemic stroke, heart failure (primary); urinary tract infection, genital infection, diabetic ketoacidosis, hypoglycemia (secondary); MACE occurrence and recurrence.
result_summary: SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with reduced risk of 30% eGFR decline (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.59-0.80, p<0.001) and 50% eGFR decline (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.45-0.80, p<0.001), with greater benefit at higher baseline eGFR (>=50 mL/min/1.73 m2). Genital infection risk was increased (HR 4.29, 95% CI 1.02-18.04, p=0.047) in patients without prior history of such infections. First MACE occurrence did not differ significantly (log-rank p=0.160), but MACE recurrence was markedly reduced (log-rank p<0.001).
short_source_excerpt: SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with significant renoprotective effects, demonstrated by reduced risk of 30% eGFR decline (HR 0.69
limitations: Single-center, retrospective design.
Observational propensity-score matching cannot fully rule out unmeasured confounding.
Genital-infection finding is based on a subgroup without prior infection history and a wide confidence interval (1.02-18.04).
uncertainty_notes: Direction is marked 'supports' for the primary renoprotective finding, but the record's own limitations/result_summary preserve the genital-infection safety trade-off -- read both together, not the direction alone.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: SGLT2 inhibitor use and disparities in all-cause mortality in type 2 diabetes: insights from a multi-ethnic population
research_question: Does the mortality benefit of SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin) use in adults with type 2 diabetes differ by ethnicity, including Indigenous populations?
claim_text: In a New Zealand multi-ethnic primary-care population with type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin use was associated with lower all-cause mortality across ethnic groups, with the largest relative benefit observed in Maori and Pacific people.
population: Adults aged 18-75 with type 2 diabetes in the Auckland/Waikato regions of New Zealand, February 2021-December 2023 (n=59,505 primary-care records, linked to national medication-dispensing and mortality records 2021-2024); 12,792 matched pairs after propensity matching.
intervention: Empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor), with funded, prioritized access for Maori and Pacific people.
comparator: No SGLT2 inhibitor dispensed.
outcome: All-cause mortality, stratified by ethnicity and by cardiovascular/renal disease/risk (CVRD) status.
result_summary: Annualized crude mortality was higher in those not dispensed SGLT2i than in those receiving it (35.2 vs 13.1 per 1000/year with CVRD; 7.7 vs 3.6 without CVRD). After adjustment, the greatest mortality difference with SGLT2i use was in Maori (HR 0.475, 95% CI 0.336-0.672, p<0.001), followed by Pacific people (HR 0.507, 95% CI 0.395-0.651, p<0.001) and European people (HR 0.667, 95% CI 0.545-0.816, p<0.001).
short_source_excerpt: the greatest difference in mortality with SGLT2i use was seen in Maori (HR 0.475
limitations: Observational, linked-records design; residual confounding and differential ascertainment across ethnic groups are possible.
Single country/health system, and specific to empagliflozin rather than the SGLT2-inhibitor class generally.
uncertainty_notes: Adds an equity-relevant finding within the SGLT2-inhibitor subtopic: the direction of benefit is consistent across groups, but the magnitude varies meaningfully by ethnicity -- worth preserving as a distinct nuance, not collapsing into a single pooled effect size.

source_title: Safety of SGLT2 inhibitors versus DPP-4 inhibitors in super-elderly patients (>= 80 years) with type 2 diabetes: a propensity score-matched cohort study
research_question: How does the safety profile of SGLT2 inhibitors compare with DPP-4 inhibitors in super-elderly (>=80 years) adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a large propensity-matched cohort of super-elderly adults with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors showed a favorable safety profile relative to DPP-4 inhibitors on most outcomes, including lower falls, fracture, and mortality risk, but higher genital candidiasis and heart-failure hospitalization risk.
population: Adults aged >=80 years with type 2 diabetes newly prescribed SGLT2i or DPP-4i, from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (176 healthcare organizations); 65,119 matched pairs after propensity-score matching (mean age 82.2, 48.7% female).
intervention: SGLT2 inhibitor.
comparator: DPP-4 inhibitor (active comparator).
outcome: Falls, hip fracture, acute kidney injury, urinary tract infection, genital candidiasis, hypoglycemia, volume depletion, hypotension, syncope (primary); stroke, myocardial infarction, heart-failure hospitalization, all-cause mortality (secondary).
result_summary: Over a mean follow-up of 269 days, SGLT2i was associated with lower risk of falls (HR 0.90), hip fracture (HR 0.78), acute kidney injury (HR 0.82), urinary tract infection (HR 0.79), hypoglycemia (HR 0.74), volume depletion (HR 0.91), stroke (HR 0.88), and all-cause mortality (HR 0.73; all p<0.05). Genital candidiasis risk was higher with SGLT2i (HR 1.70, p<0.001), as was heart-failure hospitalization (HR 1.07, p=0.007). Hypotension, syncope, and myocardial infarction did not differ significantly.
short_source_excerpt: SGLT2i demonstrated a favorable safety profile compared to DPP-4i, with significantly lower risks of falls (10%), hip fracture (22%) ... Safety concerns included increased genital candidiasis (70%) and modestly higher heart failure hospitalization (7%)
limitations: Retrospective active-comparator design; residual confounding possible despite propensity matching.
Short mean follow-up (269 days).
TriNetX multi-site network introduces site-level heterogeneity.
Super-elderly patients are historically underrepresented in randomized trials, so this fills a real evidence gap but remains non-randomized.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'qualifies' rather than 'supports' because the safety picture is genuinely two-sided: favorable on most outcomes, unfavorable on two (genital candidiasis, heart-failure hospitalization) -- both directions are preserved in result_summary and should not be collapsed into a single favorable/unfavorable label.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Comparative effects of SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists on osteoarthritis risk in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: A multi-institutional cohort study
research_question: How do SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists compare on osteoarthritis risk in adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a large propensity-matched cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with a lower risk of osteoarthritis, particularly knee osteoarthritis, compared with GLP-1 receptor agonist use.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes newly prescribed either SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists between January 2017 and December 2019, from the TriNetX database; 452,445 matched pairs after propensity-score matching.
intervention: SGLT2 inhibitor.
comparator: GLP-1 receptor agonist.
outcome: Osteoarthritis (OA) incidence over five years (primary); knee OA, hip OA, total knee arthroplasty, total hip arthroplasty, major joint injections (secondary).
result_summary: The SGLT2-inhibitor group had a significantly lower risk of OA compared with the GLP-1-RA group (HR 0.921, 95% CI 0.895-0.946), with a greater reduction for knee OA specifically (HR 0.831, 95% CI 0.783-0.882). No significant differences were observed in total hip or knee arthroplasty risk. SGLT2-inhibitor users also had fewer major joint injections (HR 0.915, 95% CI 0.882-0.951).
short_source_excerpt: The SGLT2 inhibitor group had a significantly lower risk of OA compared with the GLP-1 RAs group (HR, 0.921
limitations: Retrospective comparative-effectiveness design; channeling bias is plausible if patients selected for one drug class differ systematically in baseline OA risk or mobility.
Association study; no mechanistic validation of a causal pathway.
Residual confounding possible despite very large-scale propensity matching.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contextualizes' rather than 'supports'/'contradicts' because osteoarthritis risk is a secondary, associative safety signal rather than a primary efficacy claim about either drug class's core metabolic/weight/glycemic effect; still directly relevant to the corpus's 'clinically relevant limitations' outcome category when choosing between SGLT2i and GLP-1RA.

source_title: Comparative Effects of SGLT2 Inhibitors and GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Composite Surrogate Markers of Insulin Resistance: A Real-World Study Using METS-IR and SPISE
research_question: How do SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists compare in their effects on composite surrogate markers of insulin resistance in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity?
claim_text: In a real-world cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, both GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors significantly improved composite surrogate markers of insulin resistance over six months, with no significant difference between the two drug classes.
population: 100 individuals with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, treated with either GLP-1RA (n=54) or SGLT2i (n=46) with stable concomitant pharmacotherapy, followed for 6 months.
intervention: GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor.
comparator: The two drug classes compared head-to-head; no placebo arm.
outcome: Change in METS-IR (Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance) and SPISE (Single Point Insulin Sensitivity Estimator), alongside BMI and HbA1c.
result_summary: Both groups showed significant improvement in METS-IR (GLP-1RA -3.9 +/- 5.9; SGLT2i -2.5 +/- 2.6; both p<0.001) and SPISE (GLP-1RA +0.46 +/- 0.52; SGLT2i +0.44 +/- 0.61; both p<0.001), with no significant between-group difference. In the GLP-1RA group, METS-IR change correlated with BMI change (r=0.48, p<0.001) and HbA1c change (r=0.29, p=0.030); no significant correlations were observed in the SGLT2i group. Stratified analyses showed greater METS-IR reduction among individuals with BMI >=30 treated with GLP-1RA.
short_source_excerpt: Both treatment groups demonstrated significant improvements in METS-IR ... and SPISE ... with no significant between-group differences
limitations: Small sample (100 total, unevenly split between drug classes).
Observational, non-randomized comparative design.
METS-IR and SPISE are surrogate composite indices, not gold-standard insulin-sensitivity measures such as clamp studies.
Six-month follow-up only.
uncertainty_notes: Both drug classes improved the surrogate markers with no clear superiority at the group level; the BMI-stratified and correlation findings are exploratory and should not be treated as confirmed subgroup effects.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Precision Prescribing of SGLT2 Inhibitors in Individuals With Type 2 Diabetes for Primary Prevention of Heart Failure: Model Development and Validation Study
research_question: Can individual-level heart-failure risk reduction from SGLT2 inhibitors be predicted for adults with type 2 diabetes who do not yet have established cardiovascular, renal, or heart-failure disease?
claim_text: A prediction model combining validated heart-failure risk estimation with trial-derived SGLT2-inhibitor relative-risk reduction was developed and validated in a large UK primary-care cohort, and SGLT2-inhibitor use was associated with a lower risk of new-onset heart failure in adults with type 2 diabetes without established cardiovascular, renal, or heart-failure disease.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease; UK primary-care validation cohort with linked hospital and death records, 2013-2020 (57,368 SGLT2i initiators, 111,673 DPP-4-inhibitor/sulfonylurea comparator initiators).
intervention: SGLT2 inhibitor; model development used the SGLT2-inhibitor Absolute Benefit REsponse (SABRE) model, combining the QDiabetes-HF absolute-risk model with a trial-meta-analysis SGLT2i hazard ratio for HF hospitalization (HR 0.63).
comparator: DPP-4-inhibitor / sulfonylurea initiators.
outcome: New-onset heart failure (observed); predicted versus observed 5-year absolute heart-failure benefit (model calibration).
result_summary: SGLT2i use was associated with a 30% lower risk of new-onset heart failure (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.63-0.78), consistent with trial evidence; relative HF benefit did not vary by baseline absolute HF risk (p=0.82). The SABRE model's predicted 5-year absolute HF benefit ranged from <0.1% to 14.1% (median 1.0%, IQR 0.6-1.8%) and calibrated well against observed HF outcomes, providing more targeted HF-prevention guidance than current guidelines for this population.
short_source_excerpt: SGLT2i use was associated with a 30% lower risk of new-onset HF (HR 0.70 [95% CI 0.63-0.78]), consistent with trial evidence
limitations: The prediction model itself was built and validated on UK observational primary-care data (2013-2020), not tested in a randomized trial of the tool.
Relies on a fixed trial-meta-analysis relative-risk estimate (HR 0.63) rather than a population-specific relative-risk estimate.
Several authors disclose industry relationships (consulting/speaker fees, research funding) with SGLT2-inhibitor manufacturers, disclosed in the paper.
uncertainty_notes: Extends the corpus's SGLT2-inhibitor evidence into primary prevention (patients without yet-established ASCVD/HF/CKD), directly relevant to 'treatment response' and 'durability'/targeting questions in scientific_question.md, not just treatment effect in already-diagnosed populations.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength or the prediction model's clinical readiness.

source_title: Trends in Second-Line Initiations and Treatment Outcomes Across Age and Frailty Groups in People With Type 2 Diabetes: UK Population-Based Study, 2019-2024
research_question: As SGLT2-inhibitor use has rapidly expanded as second-line therapy in the UK, has population-level treatment outcome (glycemic, weight, and complication risk) improved correspondingly, across age and frailty groups?
claim_text: In a UK population-based cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes initiating second-line therapy 2019-2024, SGLT2-inhibitor use rose sharply across all age and frailty groups, accompanied by small population-level improvements in HbA1c and weight, but with no evidence of a corresponding change in the incidence of severe diabetes-related complications.
population: 117,046 UK adults with type 2 diabetes initiating second-line therapy between 2019-2024 (Clinical Practice Research Datalink), stratified into age <=70 (72%), non-frail >70 (16%), and frail >70 (12%).
intervention: Second-line glucose-lowering therapy, with a focus on the rising share of SGLT2-inhibitor initiations.
comparator: Trends compared across calendar years (2019 vs. 2024) and across age/frailty subgroups; not a randomized or drug-vs-drug comparator design.
outcome: Annual prescribing trends by drug class; 12-month HbA1c change; 12-month weight change; incidence of short-term severe diabetes-related complications.
result_summary: SGLT2-inhibitor use rose from 26% of second-line initiations in 2019 to 63% in 2024, with the largest increase among frail adults >70 (6% to 60%). In adults <=70, mean 12-month HbA1c response improved from -11.3 mmol/mol (2019) to -12.9 mmol/mol (2023), and mean weight loss increased from -1.7 kg to -2.8 kg. Incidence of short-term severe complications remained similar across the period (9.9 per 1000 person-years in 2019 vs 8.6 in 2022), with similar time trends across all age-and-frailty subgroups.
short_source_excerpt: there were small population-level benefits for HbA1c and weight, with no evidence of changes in complication risk
limitations: Population-level trend analysis, not a controlled treatment-effect study; cannot attribute the HbA1c/weight trends specifically to SGLT2-inhibitor uptake versus other concurrent changes in care.

Complication follow-up window is short-term relative to the years-long timescale typically needed to observe change in complication incidence, so absence of evidence for a complication-risk change is not the same as evidence of no effect.
Single country/health system (UK primary care via CPRD Aurum).
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'qualifies' because this record adds an important real-world, population-level counterweight to the individual-patient-level SGLT2-inhibitor renal/cardiovascular benefit records already in this corpus (e.g. ev-sglt2i-elderly-t2d-renal-outcomes-001): those trial-and-cohort-level effect sizes have not yet visibly translated into a measurable population-level complication-rate change in this UK data, at least not within this study's short-term follow-up window.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Network and Pairwise Meta-Analysis of the Association Between Novel Hypoglycemic Agents and Atrial Fibrillation Risk in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
research_question: How do SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and DPP-4 inhibitors compare on atrial fibrillation risk in adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a network meta-analysis of RCTs and cohort studies, SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with lower risk of atrial fibrillation and new-onset atrial fibrillation than GLP-1 receptor agonists or DPP-4 inhibitors, but there was no significant difference among the three drug classes in atrial fibrillation recurrence risk, and no significant difference between GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors on any atrial fibrillation outcome measured.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus from 4 RCTs and 21 cohort studies (2,171,267 patients total), comparing SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and DPP-4 inhibitors.
intervention: SGLT2 inhibitors (primary comparison arm).
comparator: GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors.
outcome: Risk of atrial fibrillation (AF), new-onset AF, and AF recurrence.
result_summary: SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduced AF and new-onset AF risk compared with GLP-1RA (RR 0.86 and 0.87) and DPP-4i (RR 0.80 and 0.81). There was no significant difference in AF recurrence risk among SGLT2i, GLP-1RA, and DPP-4i (RR 0.87, 0.80, 0.92 respectively, each with a CI spanning 1). There was also no significant difference in AF or new-onset AF risk between GLP-1RA and DPP-4i directly (RR 0.93 for both).
short_source_excerpt: there were no significant difference in the risk of AF recurrence among SGLT-2i, GLP-1RA, and DPP-4i
limitations: Network meta-analysis indirectly comparing drug classes across heterogeneous RCTs and cohort studies; indirect comparisons carry more uncertainty than head-to-head trials.
Mixes RCT and observational cohort evidence, which the source itself does not disaggregate in the reported effect sizes above.
AF recurrence and GLP-1RA-vs-DPP-4i comparisons are explicitly null findings with correspondingly wide confidence intervals -- absence of significance is not equivalent to proof of equivalence.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'qualifies' rather than a clean 'supports' for SGLT2-inhibitor superiority, because the favorable finding (new-onset AF) does not extend to AF recurrence, and the GLP-1RA-vs-DPP-4i comparison shows no difference at all -- the safety picture is class- and outcome-specific, not a blanket ranking of the three drug classes.

source_title: Physical Fitness with Exercise and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Treatment Alone or Combined After Diet-Induced Weight Loss: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial in Adults with Obesity
research_question: Does GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment (liraglutide), alone or combined with structured exercise, improve physical fitness outcomes in adults with obesity after diet-induced weight loss?
claim_text: In a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial in adults with obesity, liraglutide 3 mg once-daily alone did not improve physical functional performance or cardiorespiratory fitness during weight maintenance, whereas structured exercise -- alone or combined with liraglutide -- did produce fitness improvements.
population: 193 adults with obesity (age 18-65, BMI 32-43 kg/m2) without diabetes, who completed an 8-week low-calorie diet before randomization to a 1-year weight-maintenance intervention.
intervention: Liraglutide 3 mg once-daily plus usual activity (one of four randomized arms: exercise plus placebo; liraglutide plus usual activity; exercise plus liraglutide combined; placebo plus usual activity).
comparator: Placebo, structured exercise alone, and exercise-plus-liraglutide combined, across the trial's four randomized arms.
outcome: Physical functional performance (stair-climb test time), cardiorespiratory fitness (peak oxygen consumption per fat-free mass), and muscle strength (isometric knee extensor peak torque), from randomization to week 52.
result_summary: Compared with liraglutide alone, the combined exercise-plus-liraglutide treatment decreased stair-climb time by 1.2s (8.6%) and improved peak oxygen consumption by 3.0 mL/min/kg fat-free mass. Exercise alone produced similar benefits to the combined treatment, but liraglutide alone did not improve physical fitness. Relative muscle strength was higher with exercise, liraglutide, and combined treatment than placebo, driven by lower body weight with preserved absolute strength rather than a fitness-specific effect.
short_source_excerpt: Exercise alone led to similar benefits, whereas liraglutide alone did not improve physical fitness
limitations: Secondary analysis of a trial not originally powered for these physical-fitness endpoints.
Restricted to adults with obesity without diabetes; may not generalize to populations with type 2 diabetes.
Specific to liraglutide 3 mg; may not generalize to other GLP-1 receptor agonists or to tirzepatide.
This record concerns physical-fitness outcomes specifically, not liraglutide's well-established weight-loss or glycemic effects, which this study does not dispute.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contradicts' because it directly contradicts an assumption that GLP-1 receptor agonist monotherapy confers physical-fitness benefits by itself -- the source explicitly reports it did not, in contrast to exercise (alone or combined). Scoped narrowly to fitness outcomes; not a claim about liraglutide's weight-loss efficacy, which other records in this corpus address separately.

source_title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists Across the Heart Failure Spectrum: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
research_question: Do GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce the composite risk of cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalization across the heart-failure spectrum, compared with placebo?
claim_text: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized evidence across the heart-failure spectrum, GLP-1 receptor agonists did not significantly reduce the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death and first heart-failure hospitalization compared with placebo, and dedicated heart-failure trials specifically showed directional harm, even though secondary endpoints (all-cause mortality, MACE, quality of life, functional capacity) favored GLP-1 receptor agonists.
population: Adults with heart failure across the ejection-fraction spectrum, drawn from 14 studies (18,184 patients total): 6 dedicated heart-failure trials and 8 cardiovascular-outcomes-trial (CVOT) heart-failure subgroup analyses.
intervention: GLP-1 receptor agonists.
comparator: Placebo.
outcome: Primary: composite of cardiovascular death and first heart-failure hospitalization. Secondary: all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score (KCCQ-CSS), 6-minute walk distance.
result_summary: The primary composite outcome was not statistically significant (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.73-1.01, p=0.067, I2=47%). GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced all-cause mortality (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.79-0.95, p=0.008, low GRADE certainty) and MACE (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.69-0.93), and improved KCCQ-CSS by 7.4 points and 6-minute walk distance by 17.6 m. However, the mortality benefit was driven by the CVOT subgroups, while dedicated heart-failure trials showed directional harm on the primary composite outcome; the authors state the pooled mortality reduction should be interpreted cautiously given this divergence between indirect and direct evidence.
short_source_excerpt: the mortality benefit was driven by CVOT subgroups, whereas dedicated HF trials showed directional harm
limitations: Meta-analysis of heterogeneous trial types (dedicated HF trials pooled with CVOT HF subgroup analyses), which the authors themselves flag as a source of divergent direct-vs-indirect evidence.

Primary composite outcome result (HR 0.86, p=0.067) is a near-miss on conventional statistical significance, not evidence of harm overall -- the record's direction reflects that the primary hypothesis was not confirmed and that dedicated HF trials trended harmful, not that GLP-1 receptor agonists are unsafe in HF broadly.
GRADE certainty for the mortality-benefit secondary finding is explicitly rated low by the source authors.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contradicts' for the primary composite endpoint specifically. This record sits in direct tension with two 'supports'-direction records already in this corpus (ev-glp1-semaglutide-hfpef-bnp-001 and ev-glp1-semaglutide-hfref-outcomes-001), both smaller observational cohort studies showing favorable HF-related outcomes with semaglutide. That tension is preserved deliberately, not resolved here -- reconciling single-cohort observational signals against this more rigorous randomized-evidence synthesis is exactly the kind of judgment reserved for a human reviewer or a future synthesis layer, not something this record should flatten into one answer.

source_title: Association of SGLT2 inhibitors use with a lower risk of biliary diseases in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a retrospective cohort study
research_question: Is SGLT2-inhibitor use associated with a lower risk of biliary disease compared with sulfonylureas in adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a multi-center retrospective cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2-inhibitor use was associated with a lower risk of biliary disease than sulfonylurea use, with a stronger effect after long-term treatment and among higher-risk subgroups.
population: Adults aged 18-75 with type 2 diabetes newly prescribed SGLT2 inhibitors or sulfonylureas, multi-center EHR cohort from Nanjing Medical University, January 2017-September 2022 (1,901 total: 453 SGLT2i users, 1,448 sulfonylurea users).
intervention: SGLT2 inhibitor.
comparator: Sulfonylureas.
outcome: Incident biliary disease (BD); secondary metabolic and biliary biomarkers (HDL cholesterol, total bile acid, bilirubin, glycemic control, body weight).
result_summary: Biliary disease occurred in 24 of 453 SGLT2i users versus 188 of 1,448 sulfonylurea users. After inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting, SGLT2i use was associated with lower BD risk (HR 0.595, 95% CI 0.410-0.863, p=0.020), remaining significant beyond 24 months and stronger among patients over 60 years, without diabetic complications, or with high comorbidity burdens. Glycemic control and body weight were comparable between groups; SGLT2i users had higher HDL cholesterol and lower total bile acid and bilirubin levels.
short_source_excerpt: After IPTW adjustment, SGLT2i use was associated with a lower BD risk (HR 0.595, 95% CI 0.410-0.863, p = 0.020)
limitations: Retrospective, single-country/single-system EHR cohort.
Despite propensity weighting, residual confounding by indication is possible.
The biliary-biomarker mechanism reported alongside the main finding is exploratory/associative, not established as causal.
uncertainty_notes: Adds a novel, non-cardiorenal adverse-effect angle for SGLT2 inhibitors versus an active comparator (sulfonylureas) rather than placebo; the authors themselves describe the biomarker link as warranting further study, not yet established.

source_title: Treatment preference for once-weekly versus once-daily DPP-4 inhibitors in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
research_question: Does once-weekly dosing of DPP-4 inhibitors differ from once-daily dosing in treatment preference, adherence, glycemic control, and safety in adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a meta-analysis of 8 randomized controlled trials, once-weekly and once-daily DPP-4 inhibitor dosing did not differ in medication adherence, treatment satisfaction, or treatment burden, though once-weekly dosing showed a small additional HbA1c benefit and a higher risk of musculoskeletal or connective-tissue adverse events.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes from 8 randomized controlled trials (1,575 participants total) comparing once-weekly versus once-daily DPP-4-inhibitor dosing.
intervention: Once-weekly DPP-4-inhibitor dosing.
comparator: Once-daily DPP-4-inhibitor dosing.
outcome: Medication adherence, treatment satisfaction (DTSQ total score), glycemic measures (HbA1c, glycated albumin, fasting plasma glucose), adverse events, and treatment burden.
result_summary: No significant difference in medication adherence or DTSQ total score between dosing groups (p>0.05). HbA1c decreased more with once-weekly dosing (MD -0.21%, 95% CI -0.42 to -0.01, p<0.05), while glycated albumin and fasting plasma glucose showed no difference. Once-weekly dosing was associated with higher musculoskeletal/connective-tissue disorder risk (RR 2.63, 95% CI 1.18-5.83), but no significant differences in other adverse events or treatment burden.
short_source_excerpt: No significant difference in medication adherence and DTSQ total score between the once-weekly and once-daily groups (p > 0.05)
limitations: Meta-analysis of only 8 RCTs with heterogeneous designs and dosing regimens.
The musculoskeletal adverse-event finding is a single significant result amid many non-significant comparisons, raising a real risk of a false-positive from multiple comparisons.
Authors themselves note further research is needed on prescribing-behavior drivers of any real-world preference difference.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'qualifies' because the evidence is genuinely mixed: adherence/satisfaction/burden show no meaningful difference by dosing frequency, a small glycemic edge favors weekly dosing, and a safety signal (musculoskeletal AEs) favors daily dosing -- no single clean directional claim fits all findings.

source_title: Optimizing Goal Difficulty in a Digital Weight Loss Intervention: The Ignite Pilot Randomized Trial
research_question: Does harder goal difficulty (for calorie, step, eating-window, and high-calorie/low-nutrition food limits) improve weight loss more than easier goals in a digital behavioral weight-loss intervention?
claim_text: In a pilot factorial-design randomized trial of a 10-week digital weight-loss intervention, a harder calorie goal produced greater weight loss than an easier calorie goal, but harder goals for steps, eating windows, and food-quality limits showed no significant additional benefit.
population: 32 U.S. adults with overweight or obesity (mean age 47.7, mean BMI 30.1 kg/m2, 47% racial/ethnic minority) in a pilot Multiphase Optimization Strategy trial.
intervention: Harder goal difficulty (calories, steps, eating windows, or high-calorie/low-nutrition 'Red Zone' food limits), within a 10-week fully digital weight-loss intervention with daily self-monitoring, weekly lessons, and feedback, using a 2^4 factorial design.
comparator: Easier goal difficulty for the same four goal domains, within the same digital intervention.
outcome: Feasibility and acceptability (engagement, retention, satisfaction); weight loss at 10 weeks versus a priori 3% and 5% weight-loss benchmarks.
result_summary: Feasibility and acceptability benchmarks were largely met: 94% retention (30/32) at 10 weeks and 97% would recommend the program. The 3% weight-loss benchmark was met (mean -3.3 +/- 2.5 kg, or -4.0% +/- 3.6%) but the 5% benchmark was not. Participants with a harder calorie goal lost significantly more weight than those with an easier calorie goal (difference -2.3 kg, 95% CI -4.1 to -0.6 kg); no significant main effects were observed for the step, eating-window, or food-quality goal domains.
short_source_excerpt: Participants with a harder calorie goal had greater weight loss than those with an easier calorie goal (difference: -2.3 kg [95% CI, -4.1, -0.6 kg]). No main effects were observed for other goals.
limitations: Very small pilot sample (n=32), not powered for efficacy -- explicitly a feasibility/proof-of-concept trial, not a definitive efficacy trial.
Short 10-week follow-up; durability beyond this window is not assessed.
Only 1 of 4 randomized goal domains (calories) showed a significant weight-loss effect; the other three did not.
uncertainty_notes: A non-pharmacological, behavioral/digital intervention data point for the corpus's broader obesity-treatment subtopic; authors themselves frame this as needing only minor refinement before a fully powered efficacy trial, not as a completed efficacy finding.

source_title: Digital Mental Health Interventions in Obesity Management: A Systematic Review and Evidence-Based Recommendations
research_question: Are digital mental health interventions effective for obesity-related clinical, behavioral, and psychological outcomes, and does delivery modality matter?
claim_text: In a systematic review of 38 randomized controlled trials, digital mental health interventions improved behavioral and psychological aspects of obesity, often independent of weight-related improvements, with no single delivery format emerging as universally superior.
population: Adults with obesity across 38 randomized controlled trials included in the systematic review.
intervention: Digital Mental Health Interventions (DMHIs) of varying delivery modalities.
comparator: Varies by included trial; the review synthesizes findings narratively rather than reporting a single pooled comparator, and makes no claims of statistical superiority between modalities.
outcome: Obesity-related clinical, behavioral, and psychological outcomes.
result_summary: DMHIs effectively targeted behavioral and psychological aspects of obesity when grounded in evidence-based psychotherapeutic frameworks, often independently of weight-related improvements. No single delivery format emerged as universally superior; each modality appeared to serve distinct therapeutic purposes. Outcomes were more favorable in interventions incorporating human guidance, though the authors caution this finding should be interpreted cautiously given heterogeneity and the absence of meta-analytic comparisons.

limitations: Narrative synthesis only -- the review authors explicitly make no claims of statistical superiority between modalities due to heterogeneity.
High heterogeneity in study design and outcomes across the 38 included RCTs.
The 'human guidance improves outcomes' finding is exploratory, not meta-analytically confirmed.
uncertainty_notes: A non-pharmacological evidence point for the corpus's broader obesity-treatment subtopic; the review's own explicit avoidance of superiority claims should be preserved rather than compressed into a stronger-sounding summary.

source_title: Evidence That Semaglutide Represents an Important Tool for Treatment of Irregular Menses and Chronic Anovulation in Women with Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome
research_question: Does semaglutide improve menstrual cyclicity and ovulatory function in women with overweight or obesity and Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS)?
claim_text: In a single-arm prospective study of 96 women with PMOS and elevated BMI, six months of semaglutide treatment was associated with significant weight loss and restoration of ovulatory menstrual cycles in over half of previously anovulatory participants, with stronger effects in overweight and mildly obese women than in those with moderate or severe obesity.
population: 96 women with Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) and BMI greater than 25 kg/m2 completing a six-month treatment protocol.
intervention: Semaglutide, individualized dose-escalation regimen, for six months.
comparator: Within-subject pre-treatment baseline; single-arm design, no separate control group.
outcome: Body weight, fasting glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, and ovulatory function (menstrual cycle normalization and ovulation), before versus after treatment.
result_summary: Mean body weight decreased significantly (-11.3 +/- 5%, p<0.01). Of the 83% of patients with baseline oligomenorrhea and anovulatory cycles, 52.5% achieved ovulatory cycles after treatment. Results were most favorable in overweight patients (about 95% achieving menstrual cycle normalization and ovulation) and in mild obesity, but less favorable in moderate-to-severe obesity, where 25% of patients achieved normalization.
short_source_excerpt: Following treatment, ovulatory cycles were observed in 52.5% of previously anovulatory women
limitations: Single-arm, uncontrolled design -- no placebo or active-comparator group.
Findings stratified by obesity severity are exploratory subgroup results, not pre-specified confirmatory comparisons.
Six-month follow-up only; durability after treatment discontinuation is not assessed.
uncertainty_notes: Extends the corpus's semaglutide evidence into a reproductive/menstrual-function outcome domain not covered by any existing record; the severity-stratified response pattern (better in overweight/mild obesity, weaker in severe obesity) is a genuine nuance worth preserving rather than collapsing into a single effect size.

source_title: Effects of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitors on Left Ventricular Global Longitudinal Strain in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review
research_question: Does SGLT2-inhibitor therapy improve left ventricular global longitudinal strain, a marker of subclinical myocardial dysfunction, in adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a systematic review of 26 studies on SGLT2-inhibitor therapy and left ventricular global longitudinal strain in adults with type 2 diabetes, observational and before-after studies mostly reported favorable changes, but randomized and controlled studies showed more variable findings, and the authors concluded current evidence does not definitively establish a consistent treatment effect.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes across 26 studies (more than 2,300 participants) evaluating SGLT2-inhibitor therapy and reporting left ventricular global longitudinal strain (LV GLS) or LV strain, spanning heterogeneous cardiac-risk populations (preserved ejection fraction, pre-heart failure, diabetic cardiomyopathy, chronic heart failure, coronary artery disease, hypertension, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, cardio-oncology risk).
intervention: SGLT2-inhibitor therapy (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin, canagliflozin, or mixed regimens).
comparator: Varies by included study; both randomized/controlled and observational/before-after study designs are included, without a single pooled comparator.
outcome: Left ventricular global longitudinal strain (LV GLS), assessed primarily by speckle-tracking echocardiography (one study used cardiac MRI feature-tracking).
result_summary: Most observational and before-after studies reported favorable LV GLS changes after SGLT2-inhibitor therapy, while randomized and controlled studies showed more variable findings. Several studies also reported improvements in LV remodeling, diastolic function, left atrial function, myocardial work indices, NT-proBNP, and epicardial adipose tissue thickness. Certainty of evidence was limited by methodological heterogeneity, differing comparator groups, variable follow-up, non-standardized imaging protocols, and risk of bias, particularly in non-randomized and single-arm studies.
short_source_excerpt: current evidence does not definitively establish a consistent treatment effect
limitations: The systematic review's own authors explicitly note evidence certainty is limited by heterogeneity and risk of bias.
The strongest (favorable) signal comes from weaker observational/before-after study designs, while randomized evidence is more mixed -- an important asymmetry, not a uniform finding.
The review itself calls for larger, standardized randomized trials before firm conclusions can be drawn.
uncertainty_notes: Extends the corpus's SGLT2-inhibitor cardiac evidence into a specific subclinical-imaging marker rather than clinical heart-failure outcomes; marked 'qualifies' rather than 'supports' precisely because the review's own conclusion resists a clean directional claim.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the review's methodological strength.

source_title: Long-term weight loss effects of semaglutide in obesity without diabetes in the SELECT trial
research_question: Do GLP-1 receptor agonists produce sustained, long-term weight loss in adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease?
claim_text: In a prespecified analysis of the SELECT cardiovascular outcomes trial, once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg produced clinically meaningful weight loss versus placebo that continued through week 65 and was sustained for up to 4 years, in adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease but without diabetes.
population: 17,604 adults with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity, without diabetes, enrolled in the SELECT trial (Semaglutide Effects on Heart Disease and Stroke in Patients with Overweight or Obesity).
intervention: Once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg.
comparator: Placebo.
outcome: Percentage change in body weight, waist circumference, and waist-to-height ratio from baseline to week 208 (approximately 4 years).
result_summary: At week 208, semaglutide was associated with a mean body-weight reduction of -10.2% versus -1.5% with placebo (estimated treatment difference -8.7 percentage points, 95% CI -9.42 to -7.88, P<0.0001); waist circumference (-7.7 cm vs -1.3 cm) and waist-to-height ratio (-6.9% vs -1.0%) also decreased significantly more with semaglutide (P<0.0001 for all comparisons). Clinically meaningful weight loss occurred across sexes, races, body sizes, and regions, and semaglutide was associated with fewer serious adverse events but increased rates of trial-product discontinuation.
short_source_excerpt: At 208 weeks, semaglutide was associated with mean reduction in weight (-10.2%)... versus placebo (-1.5%...); P < 0.0001 for all comparisons versus placebo.
limitations: This is a prespecified secondary/anthropometric analysis of a cardiovascular outcomes trial; the trial's primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events, not weight loss.

Semaglutide was associated with higher rates of trial-product discontinuation than placebo, which could bias the observed on-treatment weight trajectory toward more adherent, possibly more responsive, participants.
Single trial, single drug and dose; population restricted to adults with preexisting cardiovascular disease, which may not generalize to lower cardiovascular-risk populations.
uncertainty_notes: Extends the corpus's semaglutide weight-loss evidence (already represented by the smaller STEP 5 trial) to a much larger cardiovascular-outcomes population and a longer, 4-year follow-up window.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the trial's methodological strength.

source_title: Effects of lifestyle and glucagon-like Peptide-1 receptor agonist-based therapies on waist circumference: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
research_question: How do GLP-1 receptor agonist-based therapies compare with lifestyle interventions (diet, exercise, or both) for reducing waist circumference in adults?
claim_text: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 intervention-comparator study arms (21 RCTs, n=3,196), GLP-1RA-based therapies and diet-alone interventions were each independently associated with significant reductions in waist circumference, but exercise-only and diet-plus-exercise arms showed more variable effects, and differences between the intervention subgroups themselves were not statistically significant.
population: Adults from 21 randomized controlled trials (27 intervention-comparator study arms, n=3,196) reporting waist circumference or visceral adipose tissue outcomes, published 2010-2025.
intervention: GLP-1 receptor agonist-based therapies, diet, exercise, or diet plus exercise.
comparator: Varies by included study arm; pooled across diet, exercise, diet-plus-exercise, and GLP-1RA-based therapy categories, without a single pooled comparator.
outcome: Change in waist circumference (cm), with exploratory associations to visceral adipose tissue change.
result_summary: Pooled across all interventions, waist circumference decreased significantly (mean difference -4.36 cm; 95% CI -4.97 to -3.74). Subgroup analyses showed significant reductions for GLP-1RA-based therapies (-5.93 cm; 95% CI -7.88 to -3.98) and diet-alone interventions (-3.46 cm; 95% CI -5.91 to -1.00), while exercise-only and diet-plus-exercise interventions showed more variable effects and subgroup differences were not statistically significant. Funnel plots suggested possible small-study effects (Egger's p=0.0025).
short_source_excerpt: Exercise-only and diet-plus-exercise interventions showed more variable effects, and subgroup differences were not statistically significant.
limitations: Subgroup comparisons between intervention types were not statistically significant despite GLP-1RA and diet-alone each being independently significant -- a genuine nuance, not a clean 'GLP-1RA beats lifestyle' finding.
The authors themselves flag possible small-study effects via Egger's test.
Meta-regression associations between baseline characteristics and response are described by the authors as exploratory and to be interpreted cautiously.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'qualifies' rather than 'supports' because the review's own subgroup analysis does not establish GLP-1RA-based therapies as statistically superior to diet-alone or lifestyle interventions for this specific outcome, even though each was independently significant.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the review's methodological strength.

source_title: Effect of pasteurized Akkermansia muciniphila MucT on insulin sensitivity, body composition, and GLP-1 production in subjects with metabolic syndrome: impact of low baseline gut Akkermansia levels.
research_question: Does daily supplementation with pasteurized Akkermansia muciniphila MucT improve whole-body insulin sensitivity in adults with metabolic syndrome?
claim_text: In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of pasteurized Akkermansia muciniphila MucT in 142 adults with metabolic syndrome, the primary endpoint of whole-body insulin sensitivity (Matsuda index) did not differ from placebo after 4 months in the intention-to-treat population, although exploratory subgroup and secondary analyses showed some significant benefits, including increased postprandial GLP-1 excursion.
population: 142 adults with metabolic syndrome, with or without prediabetes, in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter (Ireland and Germany) trial.
intervention: Daily oral capsules containing 30 billion cells of pasteurized Akkermansia muciniphila MucT.
comparator: Placebo.
outcome: Primary: whole-body insulin sensitivity (Matsuda index) after 4 months. Secondary/exploratory: HOMA-based hepatic insulin sensitivity, post-OGTT GLP-1 excursion, body weight, trunk fat, gut microbiota composition, at 3 months.
result_summary: The primary endpoint (4-month Matsuda index) did not differ between pasteurized A. muciniphila MucT and placebo in the intention-to-treat population. Exploratory subgroup analyses found that participants with low baseline gut Akkermansia levels showed, after 3 months, improved insulin sensitivity (Matsuda and HOMA-S indices) and increased post-OGTT GLP-1 excursion versus placebo (p<0.05), reductions in body weight (p=0.06) and decreased trunk fat (p<0.05); prediabetic and 63-year-or-older subgroups also showed improved HOMA-based hepatic insulin sensitivity (p=0.05) and increased GLP-1 excursion over placebo (p<0.01).
short_source_excerpt: The primary endpoint of whole-body insulin sensitivity (Matsuda index) did not differ after 4-months of daily administration... compared to placebo in the intention-to-treat subjects.
limitations: The trial's own pre-registered primary endpoint was negative; the positive findings are exploratory subgroup/secondary analyses, which carry a higher risk of false-positive findings from multiple comparisons.
Subgroup benefits were concentrated in participants with low baseline gut Akkermansia levels, prediabetes, or older age -- not the trial's overall intention-to-treat population.
Single trial; postbiotic dose, duration, and population may not generalize.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contradicts' relative to the research question because the trial's own primary, pre-registered, intention-to-treat endpoint was null; the genuine positive subgroup signals (including increased endogenous GLP-1 excursion) are recorded in result_summary and limitations rather than driving the direction label, to avoid overstating an exploratory finding as the trial's main result.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the trial's methodological strength.

source_title: Understanding reasons for initiation and experience with tirzepatide among individuals with obesity or overweight: Results from the PERCEPTIONS survey.
research_question: What motivates real-world patients to initiate tirzepatide, and what barriers do they report at treatment initiation?
claim_text: In a real-world observational survey of 518 US adults completed 4-8 weeks after their first tirzepatide dose, participants reported substantial pre-treatment disease burden and were primarily motivated to initiate tirzepatide by overall health and well-being, physical functioning, and self-confidence, while cost and insurance coverage were the most commonly reported barriers.
population: 518 US adults with obesity (BMI >=30 kg/m2) or overweight (BMI >=27 kg/m2 with at least one obesity-related complication) and without type 2 diabetes, surveyed 4-8 weeks after first tirzepatide dose (PERCEPTIONS survey, June-November 2025).
intervention: Tirzepatide (89.2% initiated at the 2.5 mg dose; 12.7% had previously received semaglutide).
comparator: None; single-arm, descriptive, real-world observational survey with no comparator group.
outcome: Patient-reported motivators and barriers to tirzepatide initiation, baseline disease burden, and ease of use, via survey instrument.
result_summary: Primary motivators for initiating tirzepatide were improving overall health and well-being (83.8%), physical functioning (58.3%), and self-confidence and/or appearance outside of work (51.4%). Common barriers to initiation included concerns about treatment cost (57.7%) and health insurance coverage (90%). Nearly half of participants had previously been unable to reduce or maintain weight loss with exercise and diet alone. Most auto-injector (98.0%) and vial (95.8%) users reported tirzepatide was easy to use.
short_source_excerpt: Common barriers to tirzepatide initiation included concerns about treatment cost (57.7%), and health insurance coverage (90%).
limitations: Descriptive, single-arm, cross-sectional survey with no comparator group; it characterizes patient experience and motivation, not treatment efficacy.

Co-authored by the drug's manufacturer (Eli Lilly and Company); a real-world survey of this kind, sponsored by the manufacturer, carries a higher risk of participation or reporting bias than an independent academic study.
Baseline-only data (survey completed 4-8 weeks after first dose); no longitudinal outcome data reported here.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contextualizes' because this record characterizes real-world patient motivation, disease burden, and access barriers around tirzepatide initiation, not a claim about treatment efficacy or safety -- a different evidence category than the corpus's existing efficacy/outcome records.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the survey's methodological strength.

source_title: Lifestyle interventions to prevent gestational and type 2 diabetes among migrant women from low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review.
research_question: Do culturally adapted lifestyle interventions prevent or improve gestational diabetes and type 2 diabetes outcomes in migrant women from low- and middle-income countries?
claim_text: In a systematic review of 8 studies (28 to 641 participants each) evaluating culturally adapted lifestyle interventions for migrant women from low- and middle-income countries, interventions combining dietary modification, physical activity, and cultural adaptation showed greater improvements in behavioral and metabolic outcomes than exercise-only or digital-only programmes, but effect sizes were modest and inconsistent, with overall certainty of evidence rated low to moderate.
population: Migrant women from low- and middle-income countries living in high-income settings, across 8 studies (28-641 participants each; intervention durations 6 weeks to 12 months) at risk of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
intervention: Culturally adapted lifestyle interventions, including bilingual delivery, culturally tailored dietary education, or community-based engagement; components ranged from exercise-only to combined diet-plus-exercise to digital/counselling delivery.
comparator: Varies by included study; standard care, no-intervention, or pre-post designs without a formal comparator arm.
outcome: Dietary behaviours, physical activity, glycaemic measures (e.g. HbA1c, fasting glucose), and diabetes-related knowledge.
result_summary: Improvements were reported across dietary behaviours, physical activity, glycaemic measures, and diabetes-related knowledge, but effect sizes were modest and inconsistent across the 8 included studies. Interventions combining dietary modification, physical activity, and culturally adapted delivery demonstrated greater improvements than exercise-only or digital-only programmes; for example, one exercise-only intervention (Kandula et al., 2016) reported a small but statistically significant increase in HbA1c (0.1%, 95% CI 0.00-0.12) rather than an improvement. Overall certainty of evidence, assessed using GRADE, ranged from low to moderate.
short_source_excerpt: Interventions combining dietary modification, physical activity, and culturally adapted delivery demonstrated greater improvements than exercise-only or digital-only programmes.
limitations: The review's own authors rate overall certainty of evidence as low to moderate and describe effect sizes as modest and inconsistent.

Only 8 studies met inclusion criteria, with heterogeneous designs (RCTs, a non-randomized controlled study, and pre-post studies without comparators), sample sizes (28-641), and outcome measures, limiting cross-study comparability.

The exercise-only counter-example (Kandula et al., 2016) is a single embedded study within the review, not the review's own pooled estimate; it is included here as an illustrative, sourced example, not a claim about all exercise-only interventions.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'qualifies' because the review's own synthesis is explicitly modest, inconsistent, and low-to-moderate certainty rather than a clean directional finding; it diversifies the evidence base beyond pharmacological interventions into behavioral diabetes prevention for an underrepresented population (migrant women in high-income settings).
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract and the specific embedded-study quote; not a confidence score for the review's methodological strength.

research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: This retrospective observational cohort study evaluated the effects of weekly tirzepatide (5–15 mg,

median treatment duration 12.7 months) on vascular function and body composition in 24 individuals [45.8%

male, median 48.6 years, body mass index (BMI) 32.3 kg/m2] with obesity and T2D. Intervention: Immediately after being diagnosed with diabetes, the

individuals received counseling and guidance on diet and exercise. Comparator: As shown in Fig. 2A, CAVI reduction tended to be greater in the

high-dose group compared to the low-dose group, although the differ­

ence did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.089). Outcome: Vascular function was assessed using

the cardio-ankle vascular index (CAVI), and body composition was evaluated using skeletal muscle index (SMI)

and body fat index (BFI) measured by InBody720.
claim_text:
Results: Tirzepatide treatment significantly decreased CAVI (post-treatment to baseline: median 8.5 to 7.8)

accompanied by significant reductions in BMI (mean 33.8 to 31.8 kg/m2), SMI (median 11.4 to 10.7 kg/m2), BFI

(median 12.8 to 11.3 kg/m2) and glycemic parameters (including HbA1c: median 6.6 to 5.6%).

limitations:
The present study has several limitations. First, it was a single-center

study with a small number of participants. Due to the small sample size,

it may have been difficult to detect statistically significant differences.

The observation period and the use of concomitant diabetes medications

were not uniform. The observed association between tirzepatide

administration and improved vascular function in this study does not

establish causality, as the absence of a control group precludes definitive

causal inference. Accordingly, these findings should be interpreted as

hypothesis-generating. Additionally, since this study population pri­

marily consisted of individuals with obesity and well-controlled dia­

betes, the findings may not be generalizable to individuals without

obesity but have poorly controlled diabetes.

nutrient intake, and neuropathy severity in 300 adults with T2DM from Northeastern Roma-

nia. Intervention: The FFQ was administered by trained personnel

through standardized interviews to minimize reporting bias. Comparator: Patients with severe neuropathy showed a higher proportion of butter/margarine con-

sumption, while animal fat intake appeared lower compared to those with mild neuropathy

(Figure 1). Outcome: Methods: Dietary intake was assessed using a validated food frequency questionnaire,

and five dietary patterns were derived using principal component analysis.

Characteristics of the Population

Neuropathy severity was significantly associated with longer diabetes duration and

higher HbA1c levels (p < 0.001 for both), indicating that disease progression and poor

glycemic control contribute to more advanced neuropathy (Table 1).
